topic: Red Sea disruption and container-shipping equity economics
capture_method: curator-frozen extracts plus unadjusted market observations

extracts: Weekly container-ship transits had fallen 67% and major carriers had suspended Suez transits.
Average Shanghai container spot rates had risen 122% since early December; Shanghai-Europe rates were up 256%.
Longer routes also increase fuel, insurance, labor, and vessel-capacity requirements, so spot-rate gains are not pure margin.
Maersk said security risk remained significantly high, cancelled some bookings, and expected delays and significant network disruption.
Service changes and Cape diversions aimed to preserve predictability, not to guarantee higher profit.
Hapag-Lloyd continued Cape of Good Hope diversions until further notice because the Red Sea remained unsafe.
The carrier repeatedly reassessed routing, leaving duration and normalization timing unresolved.
As of January 21, ten-day cumulative Suez shipping volume was almost 50% below the prior year.
Europe/Mediterranean-China freight costs had risen more than 400% since mid-November, reflecting insurance and longer-route costs.
